analysis.one_liner: Notify workers exposed to toxic workplace hazards and require employers to pay for medical monitoring.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 20 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats, the bill died in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee without a markup or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal program to tell workers — including former workers exposed up to 30 years earlier — when they had been exposed to substances that raise their risk of occupational disease, explain the risk, and connect them to counseling and medical monitoring. Employers would have had to pay for the monitoring at no cost to the worker, move workers showing early signs of disease to safer jobs with pay and seniority intact, and face penalties for firing or discriminating against notified workers. It also would have certified ten occupational health centers and funded training in occupational medicine at medical and nursing schools.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and former workers exposed to occupational health hazards — chemicals, physical agents, and industrial processes linked to chronic or long-latency diseases such as cancer. They would gain the right to know about exposures, employer-paid medical monitoring, protection from being fired for their risk status, and a paid transfer to a safer job if they show early signs of disease. Families also benefit: federal agencies running occupational disease studies would have to tell study subjects what they found [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers exposed to occupational health hazards

how_it_helps.text: Would require the government, through NIOSH, to make every reasonable effort to notify each worker in a designated at-risk population — including former workers exposed within the prior 30 years — with the hazard identified, the diseases it causes, how large the risk is compared to the general population, latency periods, and counseling information, plus a toll-free hot line [S2] [S3]

Would require the current employer to provide the recommended medical monitoring at no additional cost to the employee, and would let a worker with early evidence of disease transfer to a less hazardous job while keeping earnings, seniority, and benefits; it would also prohibit firing or discriminating against workers based on their risk status, with reinstatement, back pay, and civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation for violations [S2] [S3]

Would certify ten occupational and environmental health centers to train community doctors and nurses to recognize and treat occupational disease, and would fund grants to at least ten medical or nursing schools for occupational medicine training, backed by $25 million a year in authorized spending for fiscal 1990-1992 [S2] [S3]

Would require every federal agency that runs an epidemiologic study of occupational disease to notify the study subjects of the findings, ending the practice in which researchers learned workers were at risk but the workers themselves were never told [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers in industries using hazardous substances would bear the cost of notification, employer-paid medical monitoring, paid transfers of workers out of exposed jobs, and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing or reckless violation. Taxpayers would fund the federal side — the Risk Assessment Board, hot line, health centers, research, and training grants — at $25 million a year for fiscal 1990-1992. Employers with 50 or fewer workers would be capped at $250 per employee per year for monitoring, and those with 100 or fewer (later 50 or fewer) would be exempt from paid job-transfer requirements if making a good-faith effort to eliminate the hazard [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill builds a wall around lawsuits: notification and Board determinations could not be used as evidence in tort or workers' compensation cases, claims for mental or emotional distress based on the notices would be prohibited, and the bill's remedies would be exclusive — trading away workers' legal claims in exchange for notification and monitoring [S3] [S2]

Small employers get large carve-outs: businesses with 100 or fewer employees (50 after 1990) are exempt from medical removal protection if making a good-faith effort to eliminate the hazard, and employers with 50 or fewer pay at most $250 per employee per year for monitoring [S2] [S3]

Seasonal agricultural workers employed less than six months would get medical monitoring but no medical removal protection, so a farmworker showing early signs of disease would have no right to a paid transfer out of exposure [S2] [S3]

Coverage depends on money: the Board and NIOSH would notify only as many at-risk workers as appropriations and available science permit, and employers could seek variances exempting their workers from designation, with the exemption applying while the application is pending [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is early detection of diseases that often surface decades after exposure, when intervention is still possible — the bill's own findings argue prevention and early detection would substantially cut national medical costs [S3]. The costs to employers were deliberately restrained: small businesses largely exempted or capped, penalties set at $10,000 per violation, and the bill immunizes employers from notification-based lawsuits and emotional-distress claims, which was a major concession to business. The honest weaknesses are that the litigation shield trades one set of worker rights for another, farmworkers are left with half the protection, and whether any worker is ever notified depends on Congress actually appropriating the $25 million a year. On balance the design favors workers more than it burdens them, but it was written to be palatable to employers and still never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which asked two departments for their comments but never held a markup or brought it to a vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on March 15, 1989, joined by 19 other Senate Democrats including Edward Kennedy, Claiborne Pell, and Tom Harkin [S1] [S3] [S4]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day it was introduced [S5]
On May 12, 1989, the committee requested executive comments from the Departments of Health and Human Services and Labor — the last action the bill ever received [S5]
The committee never reported the bill, held a markup, or scheduled a vote, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have borne the cost of notification, employer-paid medical monitoring, paid job transfers, and penalties — particularly in chemical, manufacturing, and mining work — were better off because the bill died. Workers exposed to toxic substances never got the warnings or early detection the bill promised.

for.name: Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the High Risk Occupational Disease Notification and Prevention Act and assembled 19 cosponsors for it

for.name: 20 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Edward Kennedy, Claiborne Pell, and Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Edward Kennedy (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, requested executive comments from HHS and Labor, and then never reported it, held a markup, or scheduled a vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so the record shows support only from one party [S4] [S3]

industries.industry: Chemical, manufacturing, mining, and other employers using toxic substances
industries.note: The bill would have required these employers to notify at-risk current and former workers, pay for medical monitoring, move workers showing early disease signs to safer jobs at full pay, and face civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation. The bill died in committee, so these costs never arrived.

The bill's drafters carved seasonal agricultural workers out of medical removal protection, giving farm employers relief the rest of covered industry did not get; their workers would receive monitoring only through the Migrant Health Program.

industries.industry: Occupational medicine clinics and medical and nursing schools
industries.note: The bill would have certified ten occupational health centers and steered at least $1 million a year in training grants to medical and nursing schools, building a permanent federal funding stream for occupational medicine.
